title: Word Usage and Collocations
tagline: Year 2 — Which words go together: make/do, heavy/strong and fixed phrases

introduction.overview: A collocation is a pair or group of words that naturally go together. English speakers say "make a decision", not "do a decision", and "heavy rain", not "strong rain". These combinations are fixed by usage, not by logic, so they have to be learned. Word-usage questions test whether you know which word naturally accompanies another, and they also cover correct choices among similar words and prepositions.
introduction.placementRelevance: Word usage and collocation questions are commonly asked in the verbal ability section of company aptitude rounds, often in fill-in-the-blank form.
introduction.realWorldContext: Natural collocations make emails and reports sound fluent and professional; unnatural ones read as non-native.

learningObjectives: Use common verb collocations (make, do, take, have, give, pay)
Use adjective + noun collocations (heavy rain, strong tea)
Use adverb + adjective collocations (bitterly cold, fully aware)
Use group nouns (flock of sheep, herd of cattle)
Use fixed phrases and phrasal verbs

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Learn words in chunks, not alone. When you meet a new noun, note which verb and adjective go with it.

coreDefinitions: Collocation: a combination of words that frequently occur together and sound natural.
Verb + noun collocation: make a decision, do homework, take a break, pay attention, commit a crime.
Adjective + noun collocation: heavy rain, strong tea, a bitter disappointment.
Adverb + adjective collocation: bitterly cold, fully aware, deeply grateful.
Group noun: a word naming a group of animals or things (a flock of sheep, a herd of cattle).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Collocations are habits of the language. If you have often heard "heavy rain", then "strong rain" sounds wrong even though "strong" and "heavy" can both mean powerful. The only way to master them is repeated exposure, so learn them in phrases.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: When you see a blank next to a noun, ask "what verb or adjective do I usually say with this noun?" If you recall the phrase in a familiar sentence, you have the answer.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Make vs do
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: make: a decision, a mistake, a promise, progress;  do: homework, a favour, the dishes, business

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Take vs have
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: take: a break, a chance, a look, a decision (UK);  have: a break, a meal, a look
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Both are common; pick the standard one.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Adjective + noun
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: heavy rain, strong tea, heavy smoker, deep sleep, high price

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Adverb + adjective
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: bitterly cold, fully aware, deeply grateful, highly successful

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Group nouns
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: a flock of sheep/birds, a herd of cattle, a pack of wolves, a swarm of bees

mainNarrative: Start with the verb collocations. We make a decision, a mistake, a promise and progress, but we do homework, a favour and business. We pay attention, commit a crime, keep a promise, take a break and reach an agreement.
Adjective collocations: rain is heavy, tea is strong, a smoker is heavy, and sleep is deep. Adverb collocations: it is bitterly cold, we are fully aware, he is deeply grateful.
Group nouns are learned as pairs: a flock of sheep, a herd of cattle, a pack of wolves, a swarm of bees. A "piece of advice" and "a piece of information" use piece with uncountable nouns.
Phrasal and fixed expressions: a meeting is called off (cancelled); a stroke of luck is a sudden piece of good fortune; we find a solution and reach an agreement.
When two options seem acceptable, choose the one that is most common in everyday use. Revise collocations in lists and in sentences rather than as single words.

deepDiveAspects.title: Prepositions are collocations too
deepDiveAspects.content: Fond of, good at, interested in, afraid of are fixed pairs. A different preposition sounds wrong even though the meaning is clear.

deepDiveAspects.title: British and American usage
deepDiveAspects.content: Some collocations differ: take a decision (British) vs make a decision (American). In exams, the standard form is "make a decision".

solvedExamples.title: Verb collocation
solvedExamples.question: He ___ a decision after long thought. (made / did / gave / held)
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Do is for tasks and duties.

solvedExamples.title: Adjective collocation
solvedExamples.question: There was ___ rain last night. (heavy / strong / big / tall)

solvedExamples.title: Group noun
solvedExamples.question: A ___ of sheep was grazing on the hill. (flock / herd / pack / swarm)

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Say the phrase in a familiar sentence. If it sounds right, choose it.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options that sound unfamiliar with the noun.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Collocation questions are very fast if you know the phrase.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I use make and do correctly?
Can I choose heavy or strong?
Can I choose flock or herd?
